content:
Hotel owners often assume that once the commercial terms of a management agreement are settled, the difficult part is over.

In reality, that’s where the legal risks begin.

I recently reviewed a situation where a hotel owner had appointed a professional management company to oversee the day-to-day operations of the property. The agreement entitled the management company to a percentage of the hotel’s “gross revenue” as its management fee.

During the first year, the arrangement worked seamlessly.

In the second year, however, revenue declined due to seasonal factors. Surprisingly, the management fee claimed by the management company increased.

The owner disputed the calculation.

When both parties revisited the agreement, the disagreement became apparent. The management company interpreted “gross revenue” to include income from rooms, food and beverages, spa services, parking, events, and other ancillary sources. The owner believed it referred only to room revenue.

Both parties relied on the same clause.

Both believed they were correct.

The real problem was not the calculation—it was the drafting.

This is one of the most common issues I encounter while reviewing hotel management agreements. Commercial discussions may be clear during negotiations, but unless those understandings are translated into precise contractual language, disputes become almost inevitable.

A hotel management agreement should answer critical questions such as:

• What exactly constitutes “gross revenue”?
• Are GST and other statutory taxes excluded?
• How are cancellations, refunds, complimentary stays, and chargebacks treated?
• Which operational expenses are borne by the owner, and which by the management company?
• Who bears capital expenditure, repairs, and maintenance costs?
• Which decisions require the owner’s approval, and where does the management company have independent authority?
• What happens upon termination, default, or an early exit?

These provisions rarely attract attention at the time of signing because the focus is usually on the management fee or commercial terms.

Yet, years later, these are precisely the clauses that determine whether the relationship remains collaborative or ends in costly disputes.

A well-drafted agreement does more than record the commercial deal. It anticipates future disagreements and eliminates ambiguity before it can become a legal issue.

When I review or draft management agreements for hotel owners, the objective is not merely to document the transaction it is to ensure that the operational realities of the property are reflected with clarity, precision, and enforceability.

Clear drafting is often the difference between a successful long-term business relationship and prolonged contractual conflict.

Samriti Sharma
Advocate | High Court of Himachal Pradesh

comment: Beyond defining revenue, agreements should also address data ownership, audit rights, and reporting transparency. Many disputes arise when parties disagree not over terms, but over access to the numbers behind them.
